title: The Gettysburg Address: Short and Sweet
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the Gettysburg Address: the background of the Battle of Gettysburg (July 1-3, 1863) and its heavy casualties, the founding of the Gettysburg national cemetery led by David Wills, Edward Everett's two-hour oration, Lincoln's journey to town the day before and his roughly two-minute speech, myths about the speech (written on an envelope, crowd reaction, dropped mic), the speech's reframing of the Declaration of Independence and its effect on American speech and the singular "United States," textual versions, and teaching the speech in schools. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about a Kathleen (former PR contact) and Memorial Sloan Kettering's clinical trials campaign, followed by the sign-off. Opening banter covers Jean-Claude Van Damme, Blood Sport, and the film Lincoln.

segments.title: Opening banter: Jean-Claude Van Damme and Lincoln
segments.summary: Hosts chat about Blood Sport, Jean-Claude Van Damme, and the film Lincoln, which one host found dull, and a Civil War reenactment-style camp the other visited.

segments.title: Memorizing the Gettysburg Address and its brevity
segments.summary: Hosts note the speech is short, discuss whether students memorized it, and recall memorizing other texts such as Caesar's speech and a song for a play.

segments.title: Background: Battle of Gettysburg and its casualties
segments.summary: The battle from July 1 to 3, 1863, between Robert E. Lee's Confederate army and George Meade's Army of the Potomac, its heavy casualties, and its importance as a Northern victory that shifted the war's tide. Discussion of Civil War casualties compared with other wars and the Confederate markers.

segments.title: Lee's retreat and the founding of the cemetery
segments.summary: Lee retreats to Virginia on July 4 and Meade does not pursue him. David Wills, a local attorney, spearheads the national cemetery at Gettysburg, and Edward Everett is invited to speak.

segments.title: Everett's speech and Lincoln's invitation
segments.summary: Everett, a famed orator and former Secretary of State and Harvard president, was booked for the ceremony. Lincoln was invited to give brief remarks. Lincoln traveled to town the day before the ceremony and stayed at Wills's house, while some dignitaries arrived late.

segments.title: Crowd, sound, and the two speeches' length
segments.summary: Discussion of how a crowd of around 15,000 could hear Lincoln, and that Everett's two-hour speech was expected while Lincoln's brief remarks were not seen as a surprise at the time. A photographer anecdote about the mic drop is noted as likely a myth.

segments.title: Myths about writing the speech and the Lincoln bed-sharing controversy
segments.summary: The envelope-on-the-train story is discussed as probably untrue; Lincoln likely drafted in Washington with secretary John Hay. The hosts discuss a popular biography and the controversy over whether Lincoln was gay, explained by the crowded town.

segments.title: Reading the Gettysburg Address aloud
segments.summary: The hosts read the speech aloud, splitting it between them. Lincoln's text is recited in full, with a note that it is about 272 words and under two minutes.

segments.title: Lincoln's impact on American speech and the Declaration of Independence
segments.summary: Gary Wills argues Lincoln changed American oratory and writing, influencing Mark Twain. Lincoln reframed the Declaration of Independence as the foundation of the nation's ideals, and the speech changed 'the United States' from plural to singular. Hosts discuss why schoolchildren find the speech hard to grasp and the value of explaining it.

segments.title: Surviving drafts and reaction to the speech
segments.summary: Five versions are believed to exist, including copies at the Library of Congress, and the hosts discuss the reaction on the day, which may be a myth. The hosts end the speech segment with a reflection on the speech's enduring status.

segments.title: Teaching anecdote: Shakespeare professor
segments.summary: Chuck recalls a college Shakespeare teacher who explained the text line by line, arguing that such explanation helps students understand old language.

segments.title: Listener mail: clinical trials and Memorial Sloan Kettering
segments.summary: A listener letter from Kathleen, a former PR contact now working with Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, about misconceptions regarding clinical trials. The hosts discuss the topic and a possible future episode on clinical trials.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give social media and website information and sign off.
